title: Past Tense
plainEnglish: Shows that an action or state already happened or is finished.
whenToUse: Use to talk about completed past actions or past states, e.g. 어제 영화를 봤어요 (I watched a movie yesterday).
attachmentRule: Drop 다 from the stem. If the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 았어요 (가다→갔어요, 좋다→좋았어요). Otherwise add 었어요 (먹다→먹었어요, 마시다→마셨어요). 하다 verbs become 했어요 (공부하다→공부했어요). Irregular stems shift: ㄷ irregular 듣다→들었어요, ㅂ irregular 춥다→추웠어요, ㅡ drops 바쁘다→바빴어요.
contrastWith: Contrast with present V-아/어요 (지금 먹어요 = I am eating now) versus past V-았/었어요 (아까 먹었어요 = I ate earlier).

examples.en: I met a friend yesterday.
I ate bread in the morning.
I studied Korean over the weekend.
The weather was really cold yesterday.

commonMistakes: Using 았어요 after a non ㅏ/ㅗ vowel, like saying 먹았어요 instead of the correct 먹었어요.
Saying 하았어요 instead of the contracted irregular form 했어요.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Check if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ
Add 았어요 or 었어요, or use 했어요 for 하다
Apply irregular changes if the stem is irregular
beginnerExplanation: The past tense in Korean is built right onto the verb stem, and the only real choice is whether to add 았어요 or 었어요. Listen to the last vowel of the stem: if it is the bright ㅏ or ㅗ sound, you use 았어요, so 가다 becomes 갔어요 (I went) and 좋다 becomes 좋았어요 (it was good). For every other vowel you use 었어요, so 먹다 becomes 먹었어요 (I ate). The single most common pitfall is forgetting that 하다 does not follow the simple pattern; it always becomes 했어요, never 하았어요. Once vowel harmony feels automatic, the past tense becomes one of the easiest endings in Korean.

title: Future / Intention
plainEnglish: Expresses a future plan, an intention, or a guess about what will happen.
whenToUse: Use for plans, decisions, or probability, e.g. 내일 영화를 볼 거예요 (I will watch a movie tomorrow).
attachmentRule: Drop 다 from the stem. After a vowel-ending stem add ㄹ 거예요 (가다→갈 거예요, 보다→볼 거예요). After a consonant-ending stem add 을 거예요 (먹다→먹을 거예요, 읽다→읽을 거예요). ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ and take ㄹ 거예요 (살다→살 거예요). ㅂ irregular: 돕다→도울 거예요; ㄷ irregular: 듣다→들을 거예요.
contrastWith: Contrast with present V-아/어요 for current action, and with V-(으)ㄹ게요 which promises something directly to the listener rather than stating a neutral plan.

examples.en: I will go to Busan tomorrow.
I will read a book in the evening.
I will meet a friend on the weekend.
It will probably rain tomorrow.

commonMistakes: Adding 을 거예요 after a vowel stem, like saying 갈을 거예요 instead of 갈 거예요.
Writing 거에요 instead of the correct 거예요.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Check if the stem ends in a vowel or a consonant
Add ㄹ 거예요 after a vowel or 을 거예요 after a consonant
Handle ㄹ-stems and irregular stems
beginnerExplanation: This is the everyday way to talk about the future and about your plans, and it also softens into a guess when you are not certain. The form splits by sound: vowel-ending stems take ㄹ 거예요, so 가다 becomes 갈 거예요 (I will go), while consonant-ending stems take 을 거예요, so 먹다 becomes 먹을 거예요 (I will eat). When you add 아마 (probably) in front, the same ending now means a prediction, as in 아마 비가 올 거예요 (it will probably rain). The biggest beginner pitfall is spelling: it is 거예요, not 거에요, even though they sound almost identical.

title: Progressive (be ~ing)
plainEnglish: Shows that an action is happening right now and is still going on.
whenToUse: Use for actions in progress at the moment of speaking, e.g. 지금 밥을 먹고 있어요 (I am eating now).
attachmentRule: Simply attach 고 있어요 to the plain verb stem with no vowel change at all; the stem ending in a vowel or a consonant makes no difference (가다→가고 있어요, 먹다→먹고 있어요, 공부하다→공부하고 있어요). For respect toward the subject, 있어요 becomes 계세요 (기다리고 계세요).
contrastWith: Contrast with the simple present V-아/어요, which can state a habit or a general fact, while V-고 있어요 stresses that the action is unfolding right now.

examples.en: I am studying Korean right now.
My younger sibling is listening to music.
Mom is cooking in the kitchen.
I am waiting for a friend.

commonMistakes: Changing the stem vowel before 고, like saying 먹어고 있어요 instead of the correct 먹고 있어요.
Using the plain present 먹어요 when you specifically mean an action in progress right now.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Attach 고 with no vowel change
Add 있어요 to mean is in progress
Switch 있어요 to 계세요 to respect the subject
beginnerExplanation: V-고 있어요 is the Korean equivalent of the English be ~ing, and the good news is that it never changes shape with the verb. You just glue 고 있어요 onto the stem: 먹다 becomes 먹고 있어요 (I am eating) and 가다 becomes 가고 있어요 (I am going), with no vowel harmony to worry about. The reason it matters is contrast: 먹어요 alone can mean I eat in general, but 먹고 있어요 pins the action to this very moment. The classic mistake is reflexively adding 어/아 before 고, producing forms like 먹어고; remember that 고 attaches straight to the bare stem.

title: Try Doing
plainEnglish: Means to try doing something or to give something a go.
whenToUse: Use to suggest someone try an action, or to say you experienced trying it, e.g. 이거 한번 먹어 보세요 (Please try eating this).
attachmentRule: Take the 아/어 connective like in present tense. If the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ use 아 보다 (가다→가 보다, 찾다→찾아 보다); otherwise use 어 보다 (먹다→먹어 보다, 입다→입어 보다). 하다 becomes 해 보다. Then conjugate 보다 normally: 보세요 (please try), 봤어요 (tried), 볼 거예요 (will try).
contrastWith: Contrast with the plain action verb: 먹어요 just means eat, while 먹어 봐요 means give eating it a try or eat it and see.

examples.en: Please try eating this kimchi.
I have tried going to Jeju Island.
Please try on these clothes.

examples.ko: 다음에 한국 음식을 만들어 볼 거예요.
examples.en: Next time I will try making Korean food.

commonMistakes: Choosing the wrong connective vowel, like saying 먹아 보세요 instead of the correct 먹어 보세요.
Forgetting to conjugate 보다, leaving it as 먹어 보 instead of 먹어 보세요.
studyOrder: Make the 아/어 connective using vowel harmony
Attach 보다 after the connective
Conjugate 보다 for the tense you need
Use 보세요 to gently suggest trying
beginnerExplanation: V-아/어 보다 adds the meaning of trying or experiencing on top of any action verb, and it is built from the same 아/어 connective you already use for the present tense. So 먹다 becomes 먹어 보다 (try eating) and 가다 becomes 가 보다 (try going); from there you conjugate the 보다 part freely. In the present polite suggestion 먹어 보세요 it means please give it a try, while in the past 가 봤어요 it means I have tried going, which is a natural way to talk about experiences. The most common slip is leaving 보다 unconjugated, so always finish the ending, as in 보세요 or 봤어요, rather than stopping at 보.

title: Mild Surprise
plainEnglish: Expresses mild surprise or a fresh realization about something you just noticed.
whenToUse: Use when you react to something you just saw, heard, or discovered, e.g. 날씨가 정말 좋네요 (Wow, the weather is really nice).
attachmentRule: Attach 네요 directly to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel harmony (좋다→좋네요, 가다→가네요, 크다→크네요). ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ before 네요 (멀다→머네요, 살다→사네요). For past reactions use 았/었네요 (왔네요, 먹었네요).
contrastWith: Contrast with the plain statement A/V-아/어요, which simply reports a fact, while A/V-네요 adds the speaker fresh emotional reaction of noticing it now.

examples.en: Wow, you speak Korean really well.
The weather is really nice today.
The food is really delicious.
Oh, it is already this late.

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before 네요, like saying 좋아네요 instead of the correct 좋네요.
Forgetting to drop ㄹ in ㄹ-stems, like saying 멀네요 instead of 머네요.
studyOrder: Find the plain stem by dropping 다
Attach 네요 directly with no vowel change
Drop ㄹ first if the stem ends in ㄹ
Use 았/었네요 for a reaction about the past
beginnerExplanation: A/V-네요 is the little ending Koreans use to show they just noticed something, similar to saying oh or wow in English. You attach 네요 straight onto the stem with no vowel harmony, so 좋다 becomes 좋네요 (oh, it is nice) and 맛있다 becomes 맛있네요 (wow, it is tasty). It carries a soft, friendly feeling of fresh discovery, which is why it is so common in everyday conversation when you react to food, weather, or someone skill. Two things trip up beginners: do not insert 아/어 before 네요, and remember that ㄹ-stems lose the ㄹ, so 멀다 becomes 머네요, not 멀네요.

title: Seeking Agreement
plainEnglish: Asks the listener to confirm or agree with something you already believe is true.
whenToUse: Use when you expect the listener to agree, like English right? or isn't it?, e.g. 오늘 날씨가 춥지요? (It is cold today, right?).
attachmentRule: Attach 지요 directly to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel harmony (춥다→춥지요, 가다→가지요, 좋다→좋지요). It commonly contracts to 죠 in speech (춥죠?). For past confirmation use 았/었지요 (갔지요?, 먹었지요?). With nouns use 이지요/지요 (학생이지요?).
contrastWith: Contrast with a plain yes-no question A/V-아/어요?, which genuinely asks for unknown information, while A/V-지요? assumes a shared answer and just seeks agreement.

examples.en: The weather is really cold today, isn't it?
This movie is fun, right?
You like Korean food, right?
We are meeting tomorrow, right?

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before 지요, like saying 좋아지요 instead of the correct 좋지요.
Using 지요? for truly unknown information when a plain question with 아/어요? is what you really need.
studyOrder: Find the plain stem by dropping 다
Attach 지요 with no vowel change
Contract to 죠 in casual speech
Use 았/었지요 to confirm a past fact
beginnerExplanation: A/V-지요? is how Korean says right? or isn't it?, and you use it when you are fairly sure of the answer and just want the listener to agree. Attach 지요 straight onto the stem with no vowel harmony, so 춥다 becomes 춥지요? (it is cold, right?) and 가다 becomes 가지요?; in everyday speech this almost always shrinks to 죠, as in 춥죠?. The key intuition is that it assumes shared knowledge, so it feels warm and inclusive rather than truly questioning. The main pitfall is using it for information you genuinely do not know; for a real question, use a plain 아/어요? instead.

title: Subject Honorific
plainEnglish: Raises and respects the person who is doing the action, usually someone older or senior.
whenToUse: Use when the subject of the sentence deserves respect, like a teacher or grandparent, e.g. 선생님이 가세요 (The teacher is going).
attachmentRule: After a vowel-ending stem add 시 (가다→가시다→가세요); after a consonant-ending stem add 으시 (받다→받으시다→받으세요). ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ then add 시 (살다→사시다→사세요). Some verbs are suppletive and change the whole word: 먹다/마시다→드시다 (드세요), 자다→주무시다, 있다→계시다, 말하다→말씀하시다.
contrastWith: Contrast with the plain non-honorific form: 가요 simply says someone goes, while 가세요 respectfully says an honored person goes.

examples.en: The teacher is coming now.
Grandfather is eating his meal.
Mother is at home.
The boss is reading the newspaper.

commonMistakes: Using the plain verb 먹어요 for a respected person instead of the suppletive honorific 드세요.
Forgetting 으 after a consonant stem, like saying 받세요 instead of the correct 받으세요.
studyOrder: Decide if the subject deserves respect
Add 시 after a vowel or 으시 after a consonant
Replace suppletive verbs like 먹다 with 드시다
Combine into the polite form, for example 가세요
beginnerExplanation: The honorific infix -(으)시- is how Korean shows respect to the person performing the action, which is essential when you talk about elders, teachers, or customers. After a vowel stem you add 시 and after a consonant stem you add 으시, so 가다 becomes 가세요 and 받다 becomes 받으세요 in the polite present. A few high-frequency verbs do not just add 시 but swap entirely: 먹다 and 마시다 become 드시다 (드세요), 있다 becomes 계시다, and 자다 becomes 주무시다, so these must be memorized. The biggest beginner pitfall is using a plain verb like 먹어요 about a respected person; with elders you should say 드세요 instead.

title: Past Experience
plainEnglish: Says whether you have or have not ever done something before.
whenToUse: Use to talk about life experiences, like English have you ever, e.g. 한국에 가 본 적 있어요? (Have you ever been to Korea?).
attachmentRule: Make the past modifier on the stem: after a vowel-ending stem add ㄴ 적 (가다→간 적), after a consonant-ending stem add 은 적 (먹다→먹은 적). Then add 있어요 for have done or 없어요 for have never done. ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ then add ㄴ (살다→산 적); ㄷ irregular 듣다→들은 적; it often pairs with 아/어 보다 as V-아/어 본 적 있다.
contrastWith: Contrast with the plain past V-았/었어요, which reports one specific finished event, while V-(으)ㄴ 적 있다 asks generally whether the experience has ever happened in your life.

examples.ko: 저는 한국에 가 본 적 있어요.
examples.en: I have been to Korea before.
I have never worn a hanbok.
I have heard that song before.
Have you ever made kimchi stew?

commonMistakes: Using the present modifier instead of the past one, like saying 가는 적 있어요 instead of the correct 간 적 있어요.
Forgetting 은 after a consonant stem, like saying 먹ㄴ 적 instead of 먹은 적.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Add ㄴ 적 after a vowel or 은 적 after a consonant
Add 있어요 for have done or 없어요 for never
Optionally combine with 아/어 본 적 있다
beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 적 있다/없다 is the Korean way to talk about whether an experience has ever happened in your life, much like English have you ever. You first build the past modifier on the verb, adding ㄴ 적 after a vowel stem and 은 적 after a consonant stem, so 가다 becomes 간 적 and 먹다 becomes 먹은 적. Then 있어요 means you have done it and 없어요 means you never have, as in 한복을 입은 적 없어요 (I have never worn a hanbok). It very often teams up with 아/어 보다 to give V-아/어 본 적 있다, a soft natural way to ask about experience. The main pitfall is using the present modifier 가는 적 instead of the required past modifier 간 적.
